title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: Carrying out Levin's plan ran into many obstacles, but he kept at it, putting in every effort, and reached a result that, while not what he had hoped for, was enough to let him believe — without lying to himself — that the attempt had been worth the trouble. One of the chief obstacles was that the work of cultivating the land was already in full swing; it was impossible to stop everything and start over from scratch, and the machine had to be repaired while it was still running.

On the evening he got home, when he laid out his plan for the bailiff, the bailiff, with visible pleasure, agreed with everything Levin said — for as long as Levin was pointing out that all the work done up to then had been stupid and useless. The bailiff said he had been saying so for years, but nobody had listened to him. As for Levin's actual proposal — that he take a share alongside his laborers in each agricultural venture — at that the bailiff simply expressed deep gloom, offered no clear opinion, and immediately started talking about the urgent need to cart in the rest of the rye sheaves the next day and to send the men out for the second ploughing, so that Levin felt this was no time to argue it through.

When he began talking to the peasants about it, and proposing to hand the land over to them on new terms, he ran into the same enormous obstacle: they were so absorbed in the day's work that they had no time to weigh the advantages or disadvantages of the scheme.

Simple-hearted Ivan, the cowherd, seemed to grasp Levin's proposal completely — that he and his family take a share of the profits from the cattle yard — and he was fully on board with the plan. But when Levin started in on the future advantages, Ivan's face filled with alarm and regret that he could not stay to hear the rest, and he hurried off to find himself some chore that wouldn't wait: he either grabbed a pitchfork to throw hay out of the pens, or rushed off to fetch water or muck out the dung.

Another obstacle was the peasants' unshakable conviction that a landowner could not possibly have any motive other than wanting to squeeze as much as he could out of them. They were firmly persuaded that his real goal (whatever he might say to them) would always lie in what he didn't say. And they themselves, when giving their views, said a great deal but never the actual point. On top of that (Levin felt the irascible landowner had been right about this) the peasants made it their first and unalterable condition of any deal whatsoever that they would not be forced to use any new method of tillage or any new implements. They agreed that the modern plough plowed better, that the scarifier did the work faster, but they came up with a thousand reasons why neither was actually usable for them. And though Levin had accepted the necessity of lowering the standard of cultivation, he was sorry to give up improved methods whose advantages were so plain. But despite all this he got his way, and by autumn the system was working — or at least so it seemed to him.

At first Levin had thought of handing over the running of the whole farm just as it was to the peasants, the laborers, and the bailiff under new partnership terms; but he quickly saw that was impossible, and decided to divide it up. The cattle yard, the kitchen garden, the hay fields, and the arable land, broken into several parts, had to be turned into separate lots. The simple-hearted cowherd Ivan, who, Levin thought, understood the whole thing better than anyone, gathered a working gang — mostly from his own family — and became a partner in the cattle yard. A distant part of the estate, a tract of waste land that had lain fallow for eight years, was taken on with the help of the clever carpenter Fyodor Ryezunov by six peasant families on the new partnership terms, and the peasant Shuraev took over the running of all the kitchen gardens on the same terms. The rest of the land was still worked on the old system, but these three associated partnerships were the first step toward a new arrangement for the whole, and they took up all of Levin's time.

It's true that in the cattle yard things went no better than before, and Ivan strenuously opposed warm housing for the cows and butter made from fresh cream, insisting that cows need less feed when kept cold, and that butter from sour cream is more profitable, and he asked for wages just as under the old system, taking not the slightest interest in the fact that the money he was receiving wasn't wages but an advance against his future share of the profits.

It's true that Fyodor Ryezunov's company did not plow the ground twice before sowing, as had been agreed, defending themselves on the grounds that the time was too short. It's true that the peasants in the same company, though they had agreed to work the land on the new terms, always spoke of the land not as held in partnership but as rented for half the crop, and more than once both the peasants and Ryezunov himself said to Levin, "If you'd just take rent for the land, it would save you the trouble, and we'd be more free." And the same peasants kept postponing, on various excuses, the building of a cattle yard and a barn on the land as agreed, dragging it out until winter.

It's true that Shuraev would have liked to sublet the kitchen gardens he had taken on in small plots to the peasants. He plainly didn't understand — and apparently deliberately didn't understand — the terms on which the land had been given to him.

Often, too, when Levin talked with the peasants and laid out all the advantages of the plan for them, he could feel that they were hearing only the sound of his voice, and were firmly resolved, no matter what he said, not to be taken in. He felt this especially when he spoke to the cleverest of them, Ryezunov, and caught the glint in Ryezunov's eyes that gave away both ironic amusement at Levin and the firm conviction that, if anyone was going to be taken in, it wasn't going to be him, Ryezunov. But in spite of all this Levin thought the system was working, and that by keeping strict accounts and insisting on his own way, he would in time prove to them the advantages of the arrangement — and then the system would carry itself.

These matters, together with the running of the land still in his own hands and his indoor work on the book, kept Levin so busy the whole summer that he barely ever went out shooting. At the end of August he heard from the servant who brought back the side-saddle that the Oblonskys had gone away to Moscow. He felt that by not answering Darya Alexandrovna's letter, in a piece of rudeness he could not think back on without burning, he had burned his ships, and he would never go to see them again. He had been just as rude with the Sviazhskys, leaving them without saying goodbye. But he would never go to see them again either. It didn't matter to him now. The business of reorganizing his farm absorbed him so completely it was as if there would never be anything else in his life. He read through the books Sviazhsky had lent him, and, copying out what he didn't yet have, he read both the political economy and the socialist books on the question, but, as he had expected, he found nothing that touched the scheme he had undertaken. In the books on political economy — Mill, for instance, whom he plowed through first with great eagerness, hoping at every page for an answer to the questions taking him over — he found laws drawn from the conditions of European agriculture; but he couldn't see why those laws, which didn't apply in Russia, should be universal. He saw the same thing in the socialist books: either they were the lovely but impossible fantasies that had fascinated him as a student, or they were attempts to patch up, to correct, the economic situation Europe was in, with which the system of land tenure in Russia had nothing in common. Political economy told him that the laws by which Europe's wealth had developed, and was still developing, were universal and constant. Socialism told him that development along those lines led straight to ruin. And neither one gave him an answer, or even a hint of one, in reply to the question of what he, Levin, and all the Russian peasants and landowners, were supposed to do with their millions of hands and millions of acres to make them as productive as possible for the common good.

Having once taken up the subject, he conscientiously read everything bearing on it, and meant to go abroad in the autumn to study land systems on the spot, so that he wouldn't be ambushed on this question the way he had so often been on others. So often, just as he was starting to understand the idea of someone he was talking to and was starting to explain his own, he would suddenly be told: "But Kauffmann? But Jones? But Dubois? But Michelli? You haven't read them — they've worked the question out completely."

He saw clearly now that Kauffmann and Michelli had nothing to tell him. He knew what he wanted. He saw that Russia had splendid land and splendid laborers, and that in certain cases — as with the peasant on the way to Sviazhsky's — the output of the laborers and the land was great; but that in the majority of cases, when capital was applied in the European way, the output was small, and this was simply because the laborers were willing to work, and to work well, only in their own peculiar way, and this antagonism was not accidental but constant, and rooted in the national spirit. He thought that the Russian people, whose task it was to colonize and cultivate vast tracts of unoccupied land, had consciously, until all their land was occupied, stuck to the methods suited to that task, and that those methods were nowhere near as bad as people generally believed. And he wanted to prove this theoretically in his book and practically on his own land.
